info.title: Moralised Essentialism and Identity Closure in Moral Character Judgement

text.text: Accepting an excuse lowers blame, but whether it changes what observers think of the person is unsettled.
An excuse admits an act was wrong but pleads reduced responsibility.
Read as folk psychology, character accounts of excuse imply that an excuse making an act less revealing should soften judgement of the person.
Moralised Essentialism predicts otherwise.
Its central rule, identity closure, holds that once a wrong is taken to reveal who the actor is, excuses explain the act and reduce blame but leave the view of the person unchanged.
The claim is that excuses stop reaching that judgement, not that they carry less weight.

As excuses strengthen, observers should attribute the act more to the situation and blame less, while their judgements of who the actor is, and their forecasts of the actor's conduct elsewhere, barely move.
Retraction and reinterpretation, unlike excuses, change what the act was and should lower those judgements, which strict belief perseverance denies.
A proposed experiment fixes two tests beforehand.
Meaningful revision of those judgements under excuses observers credit as mitigating would reject the account.
Judgements that hold or rise after accepted retraction or reinterpretation would reject closure as the explanation of their stability under excuses.
An accepted excuse is supposed to do two things.
An observer who accepts that a wrong was done under threat should blame the wrongdoer less.
On diagnosticity accounts, which judge persons by how much an act reveals, and on character-based accounts of excuse read as folk psychology, the observer should also think better of the wrongdoer.
The first expectation is well supported (Woolfolk et al., 2006; Monroe & Malle, 2019).
text.formatted: The first expectation is well supported <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Woolfolk et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Monroe & Malle, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: I have found no study that tests the second across levels of excuse strength, with a credited excuse arriving after the person has been judged.

If an accepted excuse can lower blame while leaving the judgement of the person untouched, then explaining an act and revising a view of character come apart, and a judgement of who someone is may, once formed, stop responding to information that would otherwise revise it.
I propose that judgements of persons can behave in this way once a wrong has been taken to reveal character, and I describe an experiment that could show the proposal to be false.
Suppose Alex, an accountant, knowingly puts a false figure in a company report to defraud its investors.
After judging the act, an observer learns that her manager had threatened to fire her if she refused, that the threat was real and that she had objected in writing before giving in.
The new information explains why she acted.
It does not change what she did, or that she did it knowing it was wrong.
Nor does it show that the act was right.
The observer can accept all of it, understand the act better and blame Alex less, yet still think of her as a dishonest person who is not to be trusted with the next set of accounts.
On diagnosticity accounts of moral character, this observer's response is anomalous.
On the person-centred view, acts matter to moral judgement as signals of character, and their force depends on what they reveal about the actor (Uhlmann et al., 2015).
text.formatted: On the person-centred view, acts matter to moral judgement as signals of character, and their force depends on what they reveal about the actor <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Uhlmann et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: An act can be judged less harmful yet more revealing of bad character, because judgements of the person track diagnosticity, how much an act reveals, rather than outcome (Tannenbaum et al., 2011).
text.formatted: An act can be judged less harmful yet more revealing of bad character, because judgements of the person track diagnosticity, how much an act reveals, rather than outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Tannenbaum et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Probabilistic accounts of person perception make the point formal.

When person and situation jointly cause a behaviour, evidence that the situation produced it should weaken the inference to the person (Walker et al., 2022), provided that yielding to that situation is not itself diagnostic of character.
text.formatted: When person and situation jointly cause a behaviour, evidence that the situation produced it should weaken the inference to the person <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Walker et al., 2022)</ref>, provided that yielding to that situation is not itself diagnostic of character.

text.text: Character-based accounts of excuse, on which an excuse can work by showing that the act does not reflect bad character (Bayles, 1982; Brandt, 1985), point the same way when read as folk psychology.
text.formatted: Character-based accounts of excuse, on which an excuse can work by showing that the act does not reflect bad character <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bayles, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Brandt, 1985)</ref>, point the same way when read as folk psychology.

text.text: If the observer's view of Alex rested on this act and the excuse removes what the act revealed, the observer should think better of Alex in proportion to what the excuse shows.
The observer may instead follow a different update rule.
Once a violation has been encoded, which is to say taken to reveal who the actor is, later mitigating information still shapes the explanation of the act and still lowers blame.
It no longer reaches the representation of who the actor is.
I call the account Moralised Essentialism and its update rule identity closure.
The difference lies in reach.
Any diagnosticity account can give an excuse less weight, but closure says something stronger.
For excuses alone, and only for the judgement of who the actor is, an excuse that arrives after encoding has no effect.
Several established findings make the proposal plausible.

Moral traits are central to judgements of personal identity (Strohminger & Nichols, 2014), and negative moral behaviour can carry disproportionate weight because it is diagnostic (Skowronski & Carlston, 1989).
text.formatted: Moral traits are central to judgements of personal identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Strohminger & Nichols, 2014)</ref>, and negative moral behaviour can carry disproportionate weight because it is diagnostic <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Skowronski & Carlston, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Judgements of acts and of persons can also come apart at a single moment.

An act can be judged right while its agent is judged bad (Uhlmann et al., 2013), judgements of wrongness and of punishment draw on different features of the same act (Cushman, 2008), and blame is distinct from character judgements, which are dispositional inferences drawn from moral events rather than one of the core classes of moral judgement (Malle, 2021).
text.formatted: An act can be judged right while its agent is judged bad <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Uhlmann et al., 2013)</ref>, judgements of wrongness and of punishment draw on different features of the same act <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cushman, 2008)</ref>, and blame is distinct from character judgements, which are dispositional inferences drawn from moral events rather than one of the core classes of moral judgement <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Malle, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: On choice and capacity accounts an excuse can lower blame without improving the view of character (Moore, 1990), so a dissociation at one moment is unsurprising.
text.formatted: On choice and capacity accounts an excuse can lower blame without improving the view of character <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Moore, 1990)</ref>, so a dissociation at one moment is unsurprising.

text.text: The proposal adds a rule for change over time, and the rule applies only to excuses.
An excuse that would revise the judgement of the person before encoding fails to reach it afterwards.
Several literatures come close to identity closure.
None of them says that an excuse loses its reach once the wrong has been read as revealing the person.

Psychological essentialism is the tendency to explain observable properties by an underlying nature that supports further inferences, even when the observer cannot say what that nature is (Medin & Ortony, 1989; Gelman, 2003).
text.formatted: Psychological essentialism is the tendency to explain observable properties by an underlying nature that supports further inferences, even when the observer cannot say what that nature is <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Medin & Ortony, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Gelman, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Its components, such as discreteness, immutability, informativeness and biological basis, can come apart (Haslam et al., 2004), so no single item can show that an observer has inferred an essence.
text.formatted: Its components, such as discreteness, immutability, informativeness and biological basis, can come apart <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Haslam et al., 2004)</ref>, so no single item can show that an observer has inferred an essence.

text.text: Moral essentialism applies the same reasoning to character.
Children and adults treat moral characteristics as stable and inborn to varying degrees (Heiphetz, 2019), and essentialist descriptions of an offender increase punitiveness (Martin & Heiphetz, 2021).
text.formatted: Children and adults treat moral characteristics as stable and inborn to varying degrees <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Heiphetz, 2019)</ref>, and essentialist descriptions of an offender increase punitiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Martin & Heiphetz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Linguistics supplies the distinction the proposal needs.
Individual-level predicates attribute an enduring property to an individual, as in "Alex is a liar".
Stage-level predicates, including verbs that describe single events, attribute a property to one temporal stage of an individual, as in "Alex lied under pressure" (Carlson, 1977; Kratzer, 1995).

text.text: Noun labels lead children to judge properties more stable across time and contexts than verbal predicates do (Gelman & Heyman, 1999), and nouns support more inferences about further properties than adjectives (Carnaghi et al., 2008).

Moral character dominates impressions of persons (Goodwin, 2015), and changes to moral traits weigh especially heavily on perceived identity (Strohminger & Nichols, 2014).

Negative acts can be highly diagnostic without being read as revealing an essence. Reeder and Brewer's (1979) schematic model explains asymmetric inferences to dispositions by expectations about what different kinds of actor would do, and some traits are easier to confirm than to disconfirm (Rothbart & Park, 1986).

text.text: Where these accounts predict a stable judgement after a bad act, closure must predict something they do not (Section 6).

Work on correspondence bias shows that inferences stay tied to behaviour despite situational constraint (Gilbert & Malone, 1995), but a failure to discount the situation need not reflect a fixed dispositional inference, since it can reflect how situational information is integrated (Trope & Gaunt, 2000).

text.text: New moral information also revises impressions more than new information about sociability or competence does (Brambilla et al., 2019), so a durable first impression is not by itself evidence of a closed representation.

text.text: Closest of all is contextualisation.

When later information contradicts a first impression, automatic evaluations tend to reflect the later information only in the context where it was learned, while the first impression generalises to other contexts (Gawronski et al., 2010).
text.formatted: When later information contradicts a first impression, automatic evaluations tend to reflect the later information only in the context where it was learned, while the first impression generalises to other contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Gawronski et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Contextualisation depends on order and context and is indifferent to the kind of later information.
Extending it to explicit identity judgements takes an added assumption.
So extended, it predicts revision where the excuse was learned, and the same context-bound pattern after a retraction.
Closure predicts no revision after an excuse, even there.
If identity moves there, closure fails where contextualisation succeeds.
The present account is narrower than two neighbouring proposals.
Motivated Violation Construction (Boullineau, 2027) asks whether conduct is represented as a violation at all.
text.formatted: Motivated Violation Construction <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Boullineau, 2027)</ref> asks whether conduct is represented as a violation at all.

text.text: Identity closure takes the answer as its input.
Information that undoes the classification, such as a retraction or a justification, returns the case to that earlier question, which is why such information should revise identity.

Trait Judgmentalism (Boullineau, 2026) is a stable individual difference in which an evaluator understands credible mitigation but does not revise the evaluation of the person, a failure of weighting after comprehension.
text.formatted: Trait Judgmentalism <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Boullineau, 2026)</ref> is a stable individual difference in which an evaluator understands credible mitigation but does not revise the evaluation of the person, a failure of weighting after comprehension.

text.text: Closure concerns reach, so under closure there is no weight to get wrong.
It is claimed for population-average judgements and leaves stable differences between observers open, whereas such differences define Trait Judgmentalism.
If the closure pattern appeared only in evaluators high in Trait Judgmentalism, the individual-difference account would be favoured.
Philosophers of excuse ask what we ought to think of an excused agent, whereas the present account concerns what ordinary observers in fact think of one.

On character-based accounts, an excuse can work by blocking the inference from the act to bad character or to a defective motivational structure (Bayles, 1982; Brandt, 1985). Tadros (2005) is a pluralist, allowing defences grounded in an inability to do otherwise as well as in the act's failure to reflect character.

text.text: On choice or capacity accounts an excuse lowers blame without implying better character (Moore, 1990). Gardner (1998) holds that an excused agent met the standards of character that could fairly be demanded in the situation, which need not change predictions about the agent's dispositions.

text.text: None of these views says what should happen to a judgement of the person formed before the excuse arrived.
Excuses often come late, after the observer has judged, so order is where the present account adds a descriptive claim that these normative views leave open.
The prediction proposed here treats them as conditional claims about how ordinary observers judge.
With a stranger and a single violation the act is the only evidence about the person, which makes it plausible that an accepted excuse would revise the judgement of character.
Excuses can also cost those who offer them, who may be seen as flawed in character (Schlenker et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Excuses can also cost those who offer them, who may be seen as flawed in character <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Schlenker et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The closest empirical study discussed here examined which features of excuses damage impressions of the excuse maker (Pontari et al., 2002).
text.formatted: The closest empirical study discussed here examined which features of excuses damage impressions of the excuse maker <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Pontari et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: It is not reported as testing whether a credited excuse that arrives after the person has been judged revises that judgement.
Closure predicts that observers credit the excuse and blame less but keep their judgement of the person.
That challenges the folk reading.
It leaves untouched any account of when excuses are warranted. Strawson (1962) distinguished two groups of plea.
text.formatted: It leaves untouched any account of when excuses are warranted. <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Strawson (1962)</ref> distinguished two groups of plea.

text.text: Pleas such as "he didn't mean to" or "they left him no alternative" present the injury as one for which the agent was not fully responsible, and as consistent with the agent's attitude being what we demanded.
They do not invite the observer to see the agent as other than a fully responsible agent, and they leave the agent an appropriate target of the reactive attitudes.

Pleas such as "he wasn't himself" or "he has been under very great strain recently" suspend the reactive attitudes towards the agent as he then was, and pleas such as "he's only a child" invite the objective attitude.
The proposed Context Integration Task (Section 8) excludes pleas of strain and uses only pleas of the first group, namely external threat, coercion and lack of alternatives.
Closure predicts that the folk judgement of who the agent is survives them. Watson (1996) distinguished two faces of responsibility.
text.formatted: Closure predicts that the folk judgement of who the agent is survives them. <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Watson (1996)</ref> distinguished two faces of responsibility.

text.text: Attributability concerns whether conduct discloses what the agent is like, including what the agent is prepared to do.

Accountability concerns whether the agent may fairly be held to demands and subjected to blame and sanction. Shoemaker (2015) adds answerability, whether the agent can be asked to justify the judgements behind the act, and argues that the three can come apart.

text.text: In these terms, closure is the pattern in which judged accountability falls while predictive identity, the judgement of who the person is that supports forecasts, holds.
Judged attributability is closer to the evaluative true self, what the person values deep down, and closure predicts that true-self ratings will rise.

On an identification reading, which I adopt as an explicit assumption rather than draw from Watson's disclosure view, attributability falls where the agent does not endorse the act, as at Level 6, the strongest excuse level of the proposed task (Section 8).
Its folk relevance rests on evidence that observers hold coerced agents less responsible when they do not identify with the act (Woolfolk et al., 2006).

text.text: The mapping interprets Watson's terms and does not identify his constructs with these.
Attributability is a normative relation between agent and conduct, whereas the identity representation is a psychological state of the observer.
>The identity-closure proposal
text.formatted: <head n="3." >The identity-closure proposal</head>

text.text: An observer judging Alex keeps track of two things.
The identity representation attributes an underlying moral character to a particular person and supports predictions about that person beyond the observed event.
The occasion record holds the act in its circumstances, together with the observer's explanation of it.
Both are functional descriptions and make no claim about separate neural systems.
An observer can consistently hold both, believing that Alex is dishonest and that the threat explains why she acted when she did, because a disposition and a situation can jointly produce an act.

The identity representation corresponds to an individual-level predication that assigns the person to a moral category, and the occasion record to stage-level predications about the episode (Section 2.1).
The account's claim concerns how each is later revised.

Measures of the identity representation must also be distinguished from three nearby measures: a rating of a trait in the domain of the act (here dishonesty), a same-pressure prediction of whether the person would repeat the act in the circumstances already described, and a global evaluation.
Each generalises, so the identity measures must capture more than all three, as must unrelated-domain projection, which forecasts bad conduct in another moral domain.

Let E denote the identity representation, O the occasion record, V the violation as first described and C k the kth excuse, an item of later information that leaves the act, its authorship, the agent's knowledge and the agent's operative goal intact (Section 3.3).
Encoding produces E 0 and O 0 .
Under closure, the occasion record keeps taking in new information while identity stays fixed.
The open alternative lets later information revise identity through an update function h.
Figure 1a shows the updates each model permits.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref> shows the updates each model permits.

text.text: By reach I mean whether any path exists from information about the occasion, such as Alex's written objection, to the identity representation.
Weight is the strength of a path that exists.
A model in which an excuse merely lowers the diagnosticity of the act is an open model with a small weight.
In such a model identity still moves when the situation is learned, and explaining away, discounting one cause once another is found (Kelley, 1973), survives in weakened form.
text.formatted: In such a model identity still moves when the situation is learned, and explaining away, discounting one cause once another is found <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kelley, 1973)</ref>, survives in weakened form.

text.text: Closure therefore differs in kind from a weakened form of explaining away.
Under closure the written objection has no route to the identity representation.
Yet within one class of information an absent path and a zero weight produce the same observations, and I take this to be the account's main vulnerability.
If nothing else separated them, the two would be empirically indistinguishable.
The task narrows the problem with three comparisons, none of which rests on a flat line alone.

First, where independently elicited likelihoods imply that the strongest excuse should move identity by more than the prespecified margin (Section 9.1), the open model predicts that revision, whereas closure forbids it.
Second, retraction and reinterpretation must move the same representation within the same episode, showing that a flat line under excuses does not come from an insensitive measure.
Third, the same excuse should have more influence before encoding than after it (P3, Table 2).
text.formatted: Third, the same excuse should have more influence before encoding than after it (P3, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Beyond ordinary order effects, this separates closure from an excuse weight fixed across the episode.
A weight that encoding itself sets to zero predicts the same timing, so I treat it as closure at the behavioural level, with the mechanism, an absent path or a gated weight, left unresolved.
Closure, as hypothesised here, holds within a declared episode, which runs from the violation to the final judgement in a single session, not over a relationship or a lifetime.
Closure predicts that manipulating the excuse leaves identity unchanged.
It does not predict that identity and causal recognition, the judgement that the situation caused the act, are uncorrelated, since prior trust or construal can correlate them.

Later information about the encoded act can excuse it, justify it or deny it. Austin's (1957) distinction between excuse and justification, with outright denial added as a third kind, fixes the boundaries in advance.
text.formatted: Later information about the encoded act can excuse it, justify it or deny it. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Austin's (1957)</ref> distinction between excuse and justification, with outright denial added as a third kind, fixes the boundaries in advance.

text.text: An excuse admits that the act was wrong and that the agent did it, and pleads circumstances that reduce responsibility.
A justification accepts responsibility and denies that the act was wrong.
A denial disputes that the act occurred or that this agent performed it.
Mitigation, in the present sense, is excuse, whether partial or full, the category to which character theories of excuse apply (Section 2.5).
It cites external pressure or constraint, such as threat and costly alternatives, or else the agent's reluctance.

It leaves four things intact: the type of act, its authorship, the agent's knowledge that the act was wrong and the agent's operative goal, meaning its immediate aim, as distinct from the motive for yielding to a threat.
Reinterpretation covers justification and any information that changes what the agent is taken to have known.
Retraction is denial.
Austin counted some forms of ignorance among excuses.
The encoded act, however, is a knowing wrong, so information about what the agent knew changes the encoded act.
Counting such information as an excuse would let closure claim cases in which the act had changed, so assigning it to reinterpretation is conservative.
Closure is claimed only for mitigation.
Later conduct by the same agent is a new act in its own right and falls outside this scope.
Reinterpretation and retraction replace the original description of the violation with a revised one, from which identity is encoded afresh.
Neither equation applies.
So the account predicts that they revise identity.

This prediction separates closure from strict belief perseverance and continued influence (Ross et al., 1975; Ecker et al., 2022), taken here in a strict form on which an impression survives the withdrawal of its evidential basis unchanged.
text.formatted: This prediction separates closure from strict belief perseverance and continued influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ross et al., 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Ecker et al., 2022)</ref>, taken here in a strict form on which an impression survives the withdrawal of its evidential basis unchanged.

text.text: A fall that leaves corrected judgements above the no-violation baseline fits closure and partial continued influence alike, so the proposed experiment also compares corrected judgements with that baseline, a contrast that cannot reject the account (Supplementary Section S1.9).
A broader account would claim closure for all later information, including retraction.
That claim is not defended here.
The exploratory reanalysis in Supplementary Section S2 found revision after reframing and after later good conduct.

Its materials were classified after the results were seen, without norming, as likely to fall below the elicitation criterion for encoding (Section 4), so it is not a clean test of either version, but it makes the broader claim implausible as a default property of character updating.
The present version, prepared after that reanalysis had been seen, restricts the claim to excuses.
Each item of later information is classified by condition-level norming, a pretest of the materials, before any confirmatory data are collected (Supplementary Section S1).
A condition normed as an excuse remains one in every confirmatory analysis.
Participants' own recategorisation of the act is reported as a diagnostic and cannot move a condition out of the mitigation arm.
In the proposed study, no item is classified by its effect on identity.
The need for cognitive closure is a motivated, domain-general individual difference in the desire for a firm answer.
People high in it seize on early information and freeze on the resulting judgement (Kruglanski & Webster, 1996).
text.formatted: People high in it seize on early information and freeze on the resulting judgement <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kruglanski & Webster, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: The motivational implementation specified here assumes that high scorers process later information less, so their occasion record should also update less.
Identity closure is instead a population-average restriction on one representation, under which the occasion record keeps updating while identity does not.
If only high scorers showed the pattern, the motivational implementation would explain it better than closure does.
Closure is defined relative to an encoding event, so the account must describe that event without identifying it by the stability it is meant to explain.
A provisional description has four operations.
An observer appraises the act as a violation, judges its relevance to the actor's character, encodes it as revealing an underlying identity, and then adds later information to the occasion record.
The operations are analytically distinct, but whether they are separable in time is unknown.
Smooth updating, updating that differs across observers, or noisy all-or-none updating could produce similar average curves.
The elicitation criterion says when encoding should occur.
It is defined by features of the input.

Encoding is expected when an act is judged deliberate, diagnostic of character and intended to harm, and each property is normed separately, because a person can act deliberately under coercion while disliking the outcome.
A condition enters the confirmatory test only if its mean norming ratings meet prespecified criteria on all three.
Norming checks are made at the condition level, on the violation page and before any context is shown.
They never exclude participants.
Alex is only an illustration, and her case would itself need norming on all three.
The strongest process test concerns timing.
An excuse should have more influence on identity when it arrives before the violation is evaluated than afterwards (P3).
Structural framing (Vasilyeva & Lombrozo, 2020), which explains behaviour by social structures, should likewise prevent encoding when it precedes the violation but not reverse encoding afterwards.
text.formatted: Structural framing <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Vasilyeva & Lombrozo, 2020)</ref>, which explains behaviour by social structures, should likewise prevent encoding when it precedes the violation but not reverse encoding afterwards.

text.text: Prior positivity is treated as a covariate.
It is not allowed to become a second condition for encoding that could explain away a failed prediction.
Differences between observers threaten the population-level prediction.
Suppose some observers are closed and the rest, the open observers, revise in the same direction.
The condition means then move by roughly the open observers' change scaled by their share of the sample, so a large enough open share pushes them past the prespecified margin.
Opposite-signed changes can cancel in an average.

A scenario-level criterion (Supplementary Section S1.8) blocks cancellation across scenarios but not across observers, so the primary test can support only a population-average dissociation, and closure within each observer needs same-target trajectories and a heterogeneity criterion (Supplementary Section S3.6).
No mixture correction is applied, and a subgroup that appears stable cannot be labelled closed because its outcomes are flat.

text.text: No finding in the literature demonstrates closure, though several make it worth looking for.
Blame updates in an orderly way as evidence arrives (Monroe & Malle, 2019), and closure predicts that it stays responsive.

When the elicitation criterion is met, such conduct should be recorded as a new act, and identity should improve less than an open model calibrated on that conduct predicts.
Otherwise it predicts ordinary graded revision.
Evidence against this untested extension would leave the core prediction (P1) standing.
Since closure covers only excuses, work on corrected information bears on the retraction and reinterpretation controls.

Belief perseverance and continued influence predict the same flat line across excuses as closure.
The retraction and reinterpretation arms separate closure from their strict forms, not from partial continued influence.

Subtyping protects a broader stereotype by setting disconfirming members apart as exceptions, whereas disconfirmation dispersed across many members weakens it (Weber & Crocker, 1983; Kunda & Oleson, 1995).

text.text: Applied to one person, subtyping would set the excused act apart as an exception, and a same-target sequence of excuses could separate it from closure.
Construal failure is tested on causal recognition, the need for cognitive closure on moderation of causal recognition and identity by the need, and culpable control on blame.
For blame, Figure 1b draws one curve shared by all accounts.

text.text: A rise in causal recognition tells against construal failure as implemented, although recognising a cause does not show that it was integrated.
Culpable control holds that judgements of bad character inflate blame (Alicke, 2000).
text.formatted: Culpable control holds that judgements of bad character inflate blame <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alicke, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Its prediction is tested by comparing blame with causal recognition at Level 6 across the identity-relevant and low-diagnosticity conditions.
Any flat rating could also reflect motivated responding, because observers can be reluctant to express reduced condemnation (Geiser et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Any flat rating could also reflect motivated responding, because observers can be reluctant to express reduced condemnation <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Geiser et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Two features address this possibility, a measure of self-presentation concern taken before the scenario and a format that separates causal explanation from endorsement.
A private-versus-accountable manipulation before exposure (Tetlock, 1985) would test it directly and is left to a later extension.

text.text: The planned comparison will also fit compounds of rivals, and none is assumed to fail.
Predictive identity must also be separated from the true self.
Predictive identity supports forecasts across situations.
An observer who learns that Alex objected in writing can think better of her true self while still expecting dishonesty from her in other settings.
Under closure, true-self ratings should rise with excuse strength while predictive identity stays flat.

If true-self ratings stay as flat as predictive identity at Level 6, where the agent is normed as not endorsing the act, the predicted divergence fails, which alone does not make the two constructs identical.
If both rise, predictive identity has moved.
That is evidence against P1.
P1 carries the account, and Table 2 divides the remaining propositions by their role.

Support for several extensions cannot compensate for a failure of P1, whose preconditions are set out in Section 8.2.
P2 has an experimental form.
Conditions normed as identity-relevant and conditions normed as low in diagnosticity should differ more on unrelated-domain projection than on same-pressure prediction.
Each difference is standardised on its own latent baseline scale.
If that interaction is absent and the identity factor adds nothing to measurement or prediction, a trait-level description is preferable.
P3 establishes a discrete transition only if the timing evidence favours a change point over smooth models in which order matters.
>The Context Integration Task
text.formatted: <head n="8." >The Context Integration Task</head>

text.text: The Context Integration Task presents a violation normed as deliberate, diagnostic and intended to harm, followed by one of six levels of excuse assigned between participants.
Level 1 supplies no excuse, and Levels 2 to 5 supply progressively stronger pressure, threat or constraint.
Level 6 supplies credible severe coercion with explicit reluctance and non-endorsement.
Norming must show that observers do not see the agent as identifying with the act (Woolfolk et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Norming must show that observers do not see the agent as identifying with the act <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Woolfolk et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: P2 Representation Identity measures add information beyond the trait, global evaluation, same-pressure prediction and the evaluative true self.
An excuse has greater influence on identity before encoding than after, beyond calibrated ordinary order effects.
P4 to P7 Extension Deliberation (P4), act valence (P5), domain (P6) and delay (P7) each yield a further prediction that rests on added assumptions (Supplementary Section S3).
Levels 2 to 6 are each normed as an excuse in the sense of Section 3.3.
Each participant judges four strangers, one in each of four moral domains (honesty, and the fairness, harm and sanctity foundations of Graham et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Each participant judges four strangers, one in each of four moral domains (honesty, and the fairness, harm and sanctity foundations of <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Graham et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Two positive-control arms should move identity.
In the reinterpretation arm, later information supplies a morally good purpose that norming confirms changes whether the act was wrong.
In the retraction arm, it establishes that the allegation was false or wrongly attributed, and a check confirms that participants accepted it.
The main further conditions are a no-violation baseline, a low-diagnosticity condition and, to test P3, a condition that gives the excuse before the violation.
Identity and unrelated-domain projection are co-primary outcomes and are measured first.
Causal recognition, blame, the domain-specific trait, same-pressure prediction, global evaluation, the evaluative true self and inferred motive are measured separately.

So are factual credibility, normative mitigation (whether the information excuses and reduces responsibility), recategorisation (whether it changes wrongness) and forgiveness, since an appeal to who the agent really is may seek forgiveness rather than excuse (Attie-Picker, 2026).
The main analyses use no post-treatment selection.
Prior positivity, the need for cognitive closure and Trait Judgmentalism are measured before the scenario as covariates and candidate moderators.

The formal sequence of Section 3, successive excuses about one person, is tested directly only by a same-target sequence with a comparison group that gives only a final rating (Supplementary Section S3.6).
Supplementary Section S1 gives the full specification.
The test examines the whole trajectory of identity and unrelated-domain projection across the six excuse levels, not an average slope.
Across those levels, each may vary by no more than a small margin fixed before confirmatory data are collected (Section 9.1).
Every result is classed as invariance, revision or inconclusive.
The claim concerns average effects for the declared population of observers and scenarios.
Population-general support also requires a scenariolevel criterion, so that opposite-signed changes across scenarios cannot cancel out and mimic invariance.

No verdict in either direction is returned unless the norming preconditions hold: the violation produces an identity attribution, each excuse level raises normative mitigation above the level below, and observers do not see the Level 6 agent as identifying with the act.
A verdict also requires the uptake check, a rise in causal recognition from Level 1 to Level 6, showing that the strongest excuse was taken up.

Any verdict further requires that factual credibility ratings at every level and normative mitigation ratings at Levels 2 to 6 show observers believe the excuse and credit it as mitigating, so causal uptake alone cannot reject the account.
A failed blame check, in which blame does not fall, only withholds support.
Supplementary Section S1.8 gives the full rule.
The critical prediction has two parts, and each part is tested only while the preconditions and the uptake, credibility and mitigation checks of Section 8.2 are met.
First, identity and unrelateddomain projection must stay practically invariant across the six excuse levels.
Meaningful revision of either, under excuses that observers credit as mitigating, rejects the account outright.
Second, in the accepted-retraction arm and in the normed-reinterpretation arm, identity and unrelated-domain projection must each fall below their Level 1 means by more than the prespecified margin.
Closure is rejected as the explanation of the dissociation if, in either arm, either construct stays practically invariant or rises by more than that margin.
If both arms fail, the pattern favours strict belief perseverance or continued influence.
If only the reinterpretation arm fails, the scope rule of Section 3.3 is rejected as well.
If only the retraction arm fails, the measure has proved sensitive but the withdrawn accusation persists, so the pattern favours its continued influence (Cohen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: If only the retraction arm fails, the measure has proved sensitive but the withdrawn accusation persists, so the pattern favours its continued influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cohen et al., 2024</ref>).

text.text: An inconclusive result in either part withholds support for closure without rejecting it.
A failed construct-separation test under P2, such as a true self that stays as flat as predictive identity when the agent does not endorse the act, does not reject the dissociation.
It removes that evidence for a distinct identity construct, and a trait-level description is preferred only if the measurement and incremental prediction tests of Section 7 also favour it.
>Limitations and implications
text.formatted: <head n="9." >Limitations and implications</head>

text.text: The proposal has five serious limitations.
(1) No direct test exists, and the public data reanalysed here can neither test nor support the account (Section 5.2).
(2) Because a flexible open model contains strict closure as a special case, cross-validated predictive comparison cannot return decisive support for closure even when closure is true.
Evidence for closure must come from the trajectory test of Section 8.2.
Where open and closed models are indistinguishable, the mechanism is reported as unresolved.
(3) The prespecified margin is a fifth of a baseline standard deviation (0.20) for the full range across levels.
It is proposed without derivation, and the claim is invariance at that resolution, not an exact zero.
(4) The measures are candidate items that require validation for content, response processes, reliability and measurement invariance (Supplementary Section S1.7).
(5) Generality across cultures is open.
Causal attribution matters less to blame for interdependent observers (Park et al., 2026), and close relationships or group membership may alter both encoding and updating.
text.formatted: Causal attribution matters less to blame for interdependent observers <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Park et al., 2026)</ref>, and close relationships or group membership may alter both encoding and updating.

text.text: So may prior trust.
These factors should be investigated prospectively and should not be invoked to explain away a failed test.
What follows is conditional on the account surviving its test.
A test of relabelling would need few new materials.
Person-first labels for people who have committed sexual offences softened attitudes towards the category but did not change judgements of named individuals (Harper et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Person-first labels for people who have committed sexual offences softened attitudes towards the category but did not change judgements of named individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Harper et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Extended beyond excuses, closure predicts that relabelling after encoding changes expressed affect but not identity or unrelated-domain projection, whereas relabelling before encoding reaches identity and projection too (Supplementary Section S3).

If closure held beyond one session, an employer given a fuller explanation of an applicant's offence might keep the same expectations of the applicant, and whether such expectations matter for reintegration needs direct tests of contact, hiring and support.
The account is descriptive.

On a situationist view of character (Doris, 2002), conduct under strong situational pressure is weak evidence of robust traits, so an observer who accepts Alex's excuse and still judges her a dishonest person would, on that view, be making an error. Doris (2006 Doris ( /2021) ) uses a situationist strategy to argue that the moral psychology underlying the character theory of excuses in legal philosophy is empirically inadequate.

text.text: Whether closure is such an error or a defensible stance is a separate normative question, which the account informs by specifying which information stops reaching the judgement of the person, and when.
A second normative view points the other way.

On Watson's (1996) account, a knowing wrong can disclose what an agent is prepared to do, so an observer who still judges Alex a dishonest person may not be in error, and closure would describe a sound response to the evidence.
text.formatted: On <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Watson's (1996)</ref> account, a knowing wrong can disclose what an agent is prepared to do, so an observer who still judges Alex a dishonest person may not be in error, and closure would describe a sound response to the evidence.

text.text: This view joins two questions that the account keeps apart: whether the judgement of the person is warranted, and whether later mitigation can reach that judgement at all.
Even a warranted judgement could respond to an excuse, and a closed judgement could persist without warrant.
Alex faced a real but ordinary threat.
At Level 6, the agent instead faces credible severe coercion and is normed as not identifying with the act.
Watson's own view may still count such a knowing wrong as disclosing what the agent is prepared to do.

On the identification reading assumed here, however, attributability should fall there, because an act the agent does not endorse does not express what the agent values, and an observer tracking attributability should think better of the agent.
Closure predicts that the identity judgement holds at Level 6 as at the lower levels.
If that pattern appears, observers would not be tracking attributability on the identification reading.
I have proposed that an accepted excuse can change how an observer explains what Alex did without changing who she is taken to be.
On this proposal, the observer would blame her less and still would not trust her with the next set of accounts.
The claim concerns reach, and the Context Integration Task could reject it.
Section 8.3 states the two results that would count against it.
If a model in which excuses still make a small update fits the data as well, the question stays open.
An inconclusive result would reject nothing.
If closure holds beyond a single session, a full explanation of what someone did may leave unchanged what others expect of them in settings such as hiring or parole.
